item.text: {"schema":"voice-draft-claim-audit/4","sentences":[{"id":"p1s1","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence makes an unsupported claim about how this software is marketed and the operational benefits attributed to it.","claims":[{"claim":"Software that changes shifts at short notice is often marketed as improving staffing efficiency by reducing gaps, responding faster to demand, and producing cleaner staffing numbers.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"How commonly is short-notice scheduling software marketed with these efficiency claims?"}]},{"id":"p1s2","status":"keep","reason":"This is the essay’s interpretive thesis, characterizing retained scheduling power as control without adding an external premise.","claims":[]},{"id":"p1s3","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts real effects on workers’ prior arrangements and a causal transfer of uncertainty costs to them.","claims":[{"claim":"Short-notice schedule revisions can disrupt workers’ arrangements for sleep, care, transport, study, and second jobs and transfer the resulting costs of uncertainty from employers to workers.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that short-notice shift revisions disrupt these arrangements and shift uncertainty costs onto workers?"}]},{"id":"p1s4","status":"disclose","reason":"The metaphor rests on unsupported descriptive claims about orderly employer dashboards and workers absorbing operational disorder.","claims":[{"claim":"Scheduling dashboards can appear orderly because workers absorb the disruption produced by schedule changes.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Do scheduling systems produce apparent operational order by shifting disruption onto workers?"}]},{"id":"p2s1","status":"disclose","reason":"This asserts technical and economic effects of scheduling software beyond the request.","claims":[{"claim":"Scheduling software makes repeated shift revisions inexpensive and immediate rather than merely reporting decisions.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Which scheduling systems enable immediate revisions, and what evidence establishes that they reduce the cost or friction of making them?"}]},{"id":"p2s2","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence claims specific managerial functions, alert wording, and reduced conversational friction.","claims":[{"claim":"Managers can use scheduling software to move start times, shorten shifts, and summon staff through alerts without a direct conversation.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Which scheduling products provide these functions, and can managers use them without directly contacting workers?"},{"claim":"Some scheduling alerts asking staff to report promptly are marked “ASAP.”","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Which scheduling systems use “ASAP” in staff alerts, and how commonly?"}]},{"id":"p2s3","status":"keep","reason":"This is a value judgment about the importance of interpersonal friction and adds no external fact.","claims":[]},{"id":"p2s4","status":"keep","reason":"Calling a schedule a promise is a normative characterization, and saying a change reaches beyond work follows conceptually from workers arranging nonwork time around shifts.","claims":[]},{"id":"p3s1","status":"keep","reason":"This is a clearly signalled hypothetical question whose assumed risk is confined to the imagined case.","claims":[]},{"id":"p3s2","status":"keep","reason":"This evaluates the option within the immediately preceding hypothetical and adds no real-world premise.","claims":[]},{"id":"p3s3","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence generalizes about workers’ formal ability to decline, practical pressure, and uneven allocation of hours.","claims":[{"claim":"Workers may formally be allowed to decline scheduling updates while nevertheless experiencing practical pressure to accept them.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Under what workplace policies may workers decline scheduling updates, and what evidence shows practical pressure to accept?"},{"claim":"Work hours are assigned unevenly in some workplaces.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"How commonly are hours distributed unevenly among workers in workplaces using short-notice scheduling?"}]},{"id":"p3s4","status":"keep","reason":"This states a logical possibility within the argument: control can operate without an explicit threat.","claims":[]},{"id":"p3s5","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts that shift allocation and reputational labeling can communicate pressure without an explicit threat.","claims":[{"claim":"Employers or scheduling systems can pressure workers through fewer shifts, worse shift times, or a reputation for being unavailable rather than through explicit threats.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that declined availability can lead to fewer shifts, worse times, or an “unavailable” reputation?"}]},{"id":"p4s1","status":"keep","reason":"This is the argumentative conclusion that unpredictability constitutes control, not a separate descriptive fact.","claims":[]},{"id":"p4s2","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence makes a broad causal claim that unpredictability changes behavior before explicit instructions are given.","claims":[{"claim":"Schedule unpredictability can govern workers’ conduct before an employer gives an explicit command.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that anticipated schedule changes alter workers’ conduct without explicit commands?"}]},{"id":"p4s3","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts a behavioral consequence and identifies a real-world term for the shift sequence.","claims":[{"claim":"Workers assigned a closing shift followed by an opening shift plan their evenings around anticipated exhaustion.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows how workers alter evening plans when assigned consecutive closing and opening shifts?"},{"claim":"A closing shift followed by an opening shift is called a “clopening.”","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Is “clopening” an established term for a closing shift followed by an opening shift, and in what contexts?"}]},{"id":"p4s4","status":"disclose","reason":"This is a generalized behavioral claim about parents responding to expected schedule changes.","claims":[{"claim":"Parents who expect late schedule changes may avoid booking appointments.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that anticipated late shift changes cause working parents to avoid booking appointments?"}]},{"id":"p4s5","status":"disclose","reason":"This is a generalized behavioral claim about students responding to scheduling uncertainty.","claims":[{"claim":"Student workers may stop enrolling in classes scheduled near their possible work hours because of scheduling uncertainty.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that unpredictable work schedules affect student workers’ course enrollment?"}]},{"id":"p4s6","status":"keep","reason":"The moving fence is a coherent metaphor for boundaries repeatedly altered by the party controlling the schedule.","claims":[]},{"id":"p5s1","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts that employers encounter genuine staffing problems; calling some legitimate is evaluative, but their existence is descriptive.","claims":[{"claim":"Employers face genuine staffing problems that can justify some schedule changes.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What staffing problems commonly require employers to change already published schedules?"}]},{"id":"p5s2","status":"disclose","reason":"Each clause states a real-world occurrence not supplied by the request.","claims":[{"claim":"Employer demand changes over time.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence establishes meaningful demand fluctuations in the workplaces under discussion?"},{"claim":"Workers sometimes become ill and cannot work as scheduled.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"How often does worker illness necessitate schedule changes in the relevant workplaces?"},{"claim":"Emergencies sometimes require staffing schedules to change.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What types of emergencies require short-notice staffing changes, and how frequently do they occur?"}]},{"id":"p5s3","status":"keep","reason":"This proposes how a fair rule should distinguish narrowly defined emergencies from routine volatility; it does not claim such a rule currently exists.","claims":[]},{"id":"p5s4","status":"keep","reason":"This is a normative demand that an exception not undermine the proposed protection.","claims":[]},{"id":"p5s5","status":"keep","reason":"This is conditional reasoning: defining every ordinary fluctuation as urgent would nullify a notice requirement, while the timestamp phrase is rhetorical.","claims":[]},{"id":"p6s1","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts that short-notice scheduling causes harms in addition to lost time.","claims":[{"claim":"The harms caused by short-notice scheduling extend beyond workers losing time.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What harms beyond lost time have been documented as consequences of short-notice scheduling?"}]},{"id":"p6s2","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence makes causal claims about transport, care, and income, including income instability despite a fixed hourly rate.","claims":[{"claim":"Short-notice scheduling can cause additional transport costs, missed care arrangements, and unstable income even when hourly pay rates remain fixed.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence links short-notice scheduling to transport costs, disrupted care, and income instability at fixed hourly rates?"}]},{"id":"p6s3","status":"disclose","reason":"This asserts a causal effect on competition and worker behavior.","claims":[{"claim":"Unpredictable scheduling can make workers compete for predictable hours by displaying obedience to employer requests.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows that workers compete for predictable schedules through greater compliance or displayed obedience?"}]},{"id":"p6s4","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts that allocation systems can reward faster responses and thereby produce discipline without universal punishment.","claims":[{"claim":"Shift-allocation systems can reward workers who respond fastest, allowing employers to discipline behavior without punishing every worker.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"Do scheduling or allocation systems favor faster responders, and does that influence worker behavior without direct punishment?"}]},{"id":"p6s5","status":"keep","reason":"This is an interpretive possibility and rhetorical label derived from the argued use of allocation power, not a claim that a particular system currently operates this way.","claims":[]},{"id":"p7s1","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence makes an unsupported effectiveness claim about transparency.","claims":[{"claim":"Transparency about scheduling changes helps protect workers but is insufficient by itself.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What evidence shows both the benefits and limitations of transparency in short-notice scheduling?"}]},{"id":"p7s2","status":"keep","reason":"Recording who changed a shift and when definitionally creates a record, while that information alone logically does not confer decision-making power on workers.","claims":[]},{"id":"p7s3","status":"keep","reason":"This is a conditional evaluative inference: an appeal lacks substance under the posited condition that declining affects future hours.","claims":[]},{"id":"p7s4","status":"keep","reason":"This is a normative proposal specifying advance notice, refusal protection, and additional pay as meaningful safeguards.","claims":[]},{"id":"p8s1","status":"keep","reason":"This is a recommendation that proposed rules govern both software and supervisors.","claims":[]},{"id":"p8s2","status":"keep","reason":"This is a proposal for system design and worker protections, not a description of current systems.","claims":[]},{"id":"p8s3","status":"keep","reason":"This is a normative demand for collective access, with the stated purpose of evaluating patterns across individual records.","claims":[]},{"id":"p8s4","status":"keep","reason":"This is an information-aggregation inference expressed rhetorically: isolated records can be combined into evidence of a pattern.","claims":[]},{"id":"p9s1","status":"keep","reason":"This is a proposed enforcement principle rejecting requirements to prove intent or identify a human decision-maker.","claims":[]},{"id":"p9s2","status":"keep","reason":"This normatively identifies the factual questions that the proposed enforcement regime should treat as relevant.","claims":[]},{"id":"p9s3","status":"disclose","reason":"The sentence asserts institutional capacity to examine the listed questions.","claims":[{"claim":"Regulators, unions, and arbitrators can examine notice, consent, pay, and later opportunities when assessing automated scheduling decisions.","kind":"broad-generalization","verification_question":"What legal authority, access, and practical capacity do regulators, unions, and arbitrators have to examine these scheduling facts?"}]},{"id":"p10s1","status":"keep","reason":"This is an explicit demand that employers treat published schedules as commitments.","claims":[]},{"id":"p10s2","status":"keep","reason":"This consists of recommendations to lawmakers and labour agencies and does not assert that the proposed duties currently exist.","claims":[]},{"id":"p10s3","status":"keep","reason":"This is the essay’s evaluative characterization of unilateral flexibility as authority that imposes an uncompensated burden.","claims":[]},{"id":"p10s4","status":"keep","reason":"This is a concise value judgment defining predictability as a basic form of worker control.","claims":[]}]}
